'''Paul McEuen''' (born 1963) is an American [[physicist]]. He received his B.S. in [[engineering physics]] at the [[University of Oklahoma]] (1985), and his Ph.D. in [[applied physics]] at [[Yale University]] (1991). After postdoctoral work at [[MIT]] (1990–1991), he became an assistant professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He moved to [[Cornell University]] in 2001, where he is currently the emeritus John A. Newman Professor of Physical Science.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul McEuen |url=https://physics.cornell.edu/paul-mceuen |access-date=2025-02-27 |website=Cornell University Department of Physics}}</ref> He is an expert on the electrical properties of [[carbon nanotubes]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.news.cornell.edu/Chronicle/01/12.13.01/McEuen.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030509013352/http://www.news.cornell.edu/Chronicle/01/12.13.01/McEuen.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 9, 2003|title = Home &#124; Cornell Chronicle}}</ref> and is a member of the National Academy of Sciences.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.lassp.cornell.edu/news-detail/?page=website/news&action=show/64 |title=Cornell Laboratory of Atomic and Solid State Physics |website=www.lassp.cornell.edu |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110802202328/http://www.lassp.cornell.edu/news-detail/?page=website/news&action=show/64 |archive-date=2011-08-02}}</ref>

==Research focus==
Paul McEuen studies the electrical and mechanical properties of [[carbon nanotubes]], [[scanning probe microscopy]] of [[nanostructures]], [[molecular electronics]], and applications of nanoelectronics in chemistry and biology.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lassp.cornell.edu/lassp_data/mceuen/homepage/research.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010306141200/http://www.lassp.cornell.edu/lassp_data/mceuen/homepage/research.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 6, 2001|title=McEuen Lab Research}}</ref> His group publishes their work frequently in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' and ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lassp.cornell.edu/lassp_data/mceuen/homepage/pubs.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021021120441/http://www.lassp.cornell.edu/lassp_data/mceuen/homepage/pubs.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 21, 2002|title = McEuen Lab Publications}}</ref> and McEuen has an [[h-index]] of 90.<ref>Google Scholar on 5/14/23. https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ma8Y_ZcAAAAJ&hl=en/</ref>

==Novel==
McEuen wrote a scientific thriller, ''Spiral'' (released in 2011), in which an emeritus Cornell biology professor is murdered as part of a plot involving a biological weapon, which received positive reviews by the ''New York Times''<ref>{{Cite news
| issn = 0362-4331
| last = Maslin
| first = Janet
| title = 'Spiral,' Paul McEuen's Thriller, About a Cornell Professor
| work = The New York Times
| access-date = 2012-11-09
| date = 2011-03-13
| url = https://www.nytimes.com/2011/03/14/books/spiral-paul-mceuens-thriller-about-a-cornell-professor.html
}}</ref> and the ''Los Angeles Times''.<ref>{{Cite news
| issn = 0458-3035
| last = Corwin
| first = Miles
| title = Book review: 'Spiral' by Paul McEuen
| work = Los Angeles Times
| access-date = 2012-11-09
| date = 2011-04-18
| url = https://www.latimes.com/books/la-xpm-2011-apr-18-la-et-book-20110418-story.html
}}</ref> The German translation became available on October 29, 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.spiral-dasbuch.de/4/buchinfo.php |title=Spiral – ein Thriller von Paul McEuen - Buchinfo |access-date=2011-01-22 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101204114116/http://www.spiral-dasbuch.de/4/buchinfo.php |archive-date=2010-12-04 }}</ref> McEuen sold the movie rights for "Spiral" to Chockstone Pictures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2010/04/studio-book-buying-in-downward-spiral-leaves-dealmaking-room-for-producers-33636/|title=H'wood Studio Book Buying in Downward 'Spiral'; Dealmaking Room for Producers|date=20 April 2010}}</ref>

==Positions==
* John A. Newman (formerly Goldwin Smith) Professor of Physics, [[Cornell University]], (2008–present)
* Professor, physics, [[Cornell University]], (2001–present)
* Associate professor, Physics, [[University of California, Berkeley]] (1996-2000)
* Assistant professor, Physics, [[University of California, Berkeley]] (1992-1996)
* Postdoctoral researcher, [[MIT]] (1990-1991)

==Awards and fellowships==
* [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (2011)
* [[American Physical Society]] Fellow (2003)
* Agilent Technologies [[Europhysics Prize]] (2001)
* [[Packard Foundation]] Interdisciplinary Fellow (1999)
* [[LBNL]] Outstanding Performance Award (1997)
* National Young Investigator (1993-1998)
* [[Packard Foundation]] Fellow (1992-1997)
* [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] Fellow (1992-1994)
* [[Office of Naval Research]] Young Investigator (1992-1995)

==Other contributions==
* McEuen has written ''Chapter 18, Nanostructures'' of [[Charles Kittel|Kittel]]'s famous textbook ''[[Introduction to Solid State Physics]]'' (8ed).<ref>{{cite book |last=Kittel |first=Charles |title=Introduction to Solid State Physics |date=11 November 2004 |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780471415268 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-471-41526-8 |edition=8 |url-access=registration }}</ref>
* McEuen, along with others, helped uncover the [[Schön scandal]].<ref name=Cassuto>{{cite web |website=[[Salon.com]] |last=Cassuto |first=Leonard |title=Big trouble in the world of "Big Physics" |date=16 September 2002 |url=http://dir.salon.com/story/tech/feature/2002/09/16/physics/index.html# |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080925065126/http://dir.salon.com/story/tech/feature/2002/09/16/physics/index.html |archive-date=25 September 2008 }}</ref>
